concepts.description: System software that manages hardware resources and provides abstractions to applications.
The OS technique of creating convenient virtual forms of physical resources.
The set of problems and techniques involved when multiple activities execute at overlapping times.
The OS support for keeping data intact across crashes, power loss, and program termination.
The role of an OS in allocating and coordinating CPU, memory, storage, and devices.
The operating system activity of assigning limited resources such as CPU time, memory, and I/O devices to processes or threads.
A controlled interface through which user programs request OS services.
A defined interface used by programs to request services from software such as the OS.
A restricted CPU execution mode used for ordinary application code.
A privileged CPU execution mode that allows the OS to execute protected instructions.
A controlled transfer from user mode to the kernel, often used to implement system calls.
An event that causes the CPU to transfer control to the OS or an interrupt handler.
A synchronous event caused by executing an instruction, often requiring OS handling.
A high-level algorithm or rule used by the OS to make decisions.
A low-level method or implementation technique used to provide a system function.
A simplified interface that hides lower-level implementation details.
The OS illusion that many programs each have their own CPU despite limited physical CPUs.
An executing program along with its address space, registers, and OS-managed state.
A passive set of instructions and static data that becomes a process when executed.
The current scheduling or execution condition of a process such as running, ready, or blocked.
The state in which a process is currently executing on a CPU.
The state in which a process is ready to run but not currently selected by the scheduler.
The state in which a process cannot run until an event such as I/O completion occurs.
An OS data structure that stores the state and metadata of a process.
The OS mechanism of saving one execution context and restoring another.
The OS component that selects which ready process or thread should run next.
The decision rule used by the scheduler to choose the next job or process.
A technique that rapidly switches the CPU among tasks to create the illusion of simultaneity.
A technique that partitions a resource spatially among users or objects.
Keeping multiple programs in memory and switching among them to improve CPU utilization.
A computing mode in which jobs are collected and run without interactive user control.
The responsiveness of a system to user input and ongoing interaction.
The total time from job arrival to completion.
The time from job arrival or request submission until the first response.
The amount of work completed per unit time.
A scheduling policy that runs jobs in arrival order.
A scheduling policy that runs the job with the shortest expected run time first.
A preemptive scheduling policy that runs the job with the least remaining time.
A preemptive scheduling policy that cycles through ready tasks using a time quantum.
The fixed CPU interval assigned to a task before preemption may occur.
A scheduler that uses multiple priority queues and changes priorities based on observed behavior.
A scheduling approach that selects tasks according to priority values.
The ability of the OS to interrupt a running task and switch to another task.
A Unix system call that creates a new process by duplicating the calling process.
A Unix system call family that replaces the current process image with a new program.
A Unix system call used by a parent process to wait for a child process to change state or exit.
A terminated process that still has an entry because its parent has not collected its exit status.
The OS and hardware mechanism that gives each process a private virtual address space.
The memory abstraction containing a process's code, stack, heap, and other memory regions.
An address generated by a program before translation to a physical address.
An address used to access actual physical memory hardware.
The process of converting a virtual address into a physical address.
A simple dynamic relocation mechanism using base and bounds registers.
A memory virtualization technique that divides an address space into variable-sized segments.
A memory management technique that divides virtual memory into fixed-size pages.
A fixed-size block of virtual memory used in paging.
A fixed-size block of physical memory that can hold a virtual page.
A per-process data structure that maps virtual pages to physical frames.
An entry in a page table that records translation and protection metadata.
A hardware cache that speeds up virtual-to-physical address translation.
An event in which a translation is not found in the TLB and must be resolved.
A hardware tag that lets TLB entries from multiple address spaces coexist safely.
A page table organization that reduces memory overhead by using multiple levels of tables.
An exception raised when a referenced virtual page is not currently mapped or resident.
Moving pages or processes between memory and storage to manage limited physical memory.
Loading pages into physical memory only when they are actually accessed.
The policy for choosing which memory page to evict when physical memory is full.
A replacement policy that evicts the page that has not been used for the longest time.
A page replacement policy that evicts pages in the order they entered memory.
An approximate LRU page replacement algorithm using reference bits.
A state where excessive paging causes severe performance degradation.
Wasted space inside an allocated fixed-size block such as a page.
Wasted free space split into small pieces between allocated regions.
A process memory region used for dynamically allocated objects.
A process or thread memory region used for call frames, local variables, and return addresses.
A C library call that requests heap memory allocation.
A C library call that releases previously allocated heap memory.
A bug where allocated memory is no longer useful but is not released.
A bug where a program writes beyond the bounds of an allocated buffer.
A pointer that refers to memory that has already been freed or invalidated.
An independent execution stream within a process that shares the process address space.
A programming model where multiple threads execute within one process.
An OS or runtime data structure that stores a thread's execution state.
Storage that is private to each thread even within a shared address space.
The POSIX threading API used to create and synchronize threads.
A bug where program results depend on uncontrolled timing between concurrent executions.
A code region that accesses shared state and must not be executed concurrently by multiple threads.
The property that at most one thread can execute a critical section at a time.
The property that an operation appears to execute all at once or not at all.
Techniques for coordinating concurrent threads or processes.
A synchronization primitive used to enforce mutual exclusion.
A lock-like synchronization object that allows one thread to enter a critical section.
A lock that repeatedly checks until it becomes available instead of sleeping.
A synchronization primitive that lets threads sleep until a condition becomes true.
A synchronization abstraction that combines mutual exclusion with condition-based waiting.
A synchronization primitive with a counter used for mutual exclusion or ordering.
A state in which a set of threads or processes wait forever for one another.
A state in which tasks keep changing state in response to each other but make no progress.
A condition where a process or thread waits indefinitely because resources are repeatedly given to others.
A classic synchronization problem involving producers adding items and consumers removing them.
A synchronization mechanism allowing multiple readers or one writer.
An atomic hardware instruction commonly used to implement locks.
An atomic instruction that updates a value only if it still equals an expected value.
Hardware that provides input, output, or storage services to the computer system.
Kernel software that encapsulates device-specific control logic behind a common interface.
Repeatedly checking device status until it is ready or an event occurs.
A data transfer method where the CPU explicitly moves data to or from a device.
A mechanism that lets devices transfer data to or from memory without CPU copying.
Kernel code that runs in response to an interrupt.
A device communication method that exposes device registers as memory addresses.
A hardware register through which software observes or controls a device.
A persistent storage device that stores data magnetically on rotating platters.
A persistent storage device based on flash memory rather than rotating media.
A small addressable unit of disk storage, traditionally 512 bytes.
A circular path on a disk platter that contains sectors.
The time needed to move a disk head to the required track.
The time spent waiting for the desired disk sector to rotate under the head.
Policies that order disk requests to improve performance.
A storage technique that combines multiple disks for performance, capacity, or reliability.
OS software that organizes, names, stores, and retrieves persistent files and directories.
A named collection of persistent data managed by a file system.
A file system object that maps names to files or other directories.
A string that identifies a file or directory location in a namespace.
A per-process integer handle used by Unix-like systems to refer to an open file.
The system call operations for obtaining and releasing access to a file.
System call operations for transferring data between files and process memory.
A file system metadata object that records attributes and block pointers for a file.
A fixed-size storage unit used by a file system to hold file data or metadata.
A compact metadata structure used to track free or allocated blocks or inodes.
The file system task of tracking which storage blocks or inodes are available.
The operation of attaching a file system to a point in a single directory tree.
The property that on-disk file system structures agree after updates or crashes.
Ensuring a file system remains recoverable and consistent after a crash.
A crash-consistency technique that records intended updates in a journal before applying them.
A technique that writes modified data to new locations before redirecting references.
A tool that checks and repairs file system inconsistencies after an unclean shutdown.
A stateless network file system protocol originally developed by Sun.
A distributed file system using client caching and server-managed callbacks.
A protocol-level identifier used to refer to a file or directory in a network file system.
